Pilot Sample Size for a Two Stage Fixed Width Interval for a Normal Mean

Source: R/ts_fwd_norm_mean.R
ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot.Rd

Returns the first stage (pilot) sample size for Stein's two stage fixed width confidence interval for the mean of a normal distribution, evaluated by ts_fwd_norm_mean. The interval is \(\bar{X} \pm d\): d is the half width (the margin of error), so the full width is \(2d\).

Usage

ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d, conf_level = 0.95, m_0 = 10, gamma = 1)

Arguments

d

The half width of the confidence interval (the margin of error), in the units of the data. A single positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level, strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

m_0

The smallest first stage sample size to return. A whole number of at least 2 (a variance needs two observations). Default 10; see Details.

gamma

Positive tuning constant of the pilot rule. Larger values give a smaller first stage. Default 1, for which the rule is \(\lceil z_{\alpha/2} / d \rceil\).

Value

A length one integer: the first stage sample size.

Details

The pilot size is $$m = \max\{m_0,\ \lceil (z_{\alpha/2} / d)^{2/(1 + \gamma)} \rceil\},$$ where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the standard normal quantile for the confidence level. The sample size that would be used if the variance \(\sigma^2\) were known is \(C = z_{\alpha/2}^2 \sigma^2 / d^2\) (see seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal); the rule raises the constant \((z_{\alpha/2} / d)^2\) to the power \(1/(1 + \gamma)\), so the first stage grows as the target narrows but more slowly than \(C\) does. This is the form of pilot that Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, Equation 24) recommend, following Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), for a purely sequential procedure. Using it here, with the known variance sample size for \(\sigma = 1\) as the constant, is this package's choice and not part of Stein's procedure, which is valid for any first stage of at least two observations.

The minimum m_0 matters more than the rule. Stein's procedure pays for not knowing the variance through the t quantile on \(m - 1\) degrees of freedom, so the expected total sample size is about \(t_{m-1,\alpha/2}^2 / z_{\alpha/2}^2\) times \(C\). At a confidence level of 0.95 that ratio is 42.0 for \(m = 2\), 4.82 for \(m = 3\), 2.01 for \(m = 5\), 1.33 for \(m = 10\), 1.14 for \(m = 20\), and 1.09 for \(m = 30\). The default m_0 = 10 holds the expected total to about 1.33 times \(C\) at 0.95 (about 1.6 times \(C\) at 0.99). A first stage larger than \(C\) is wasted, so lower m_0 only when even ten observations may be more than the study needs.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

Stein, C. (1945). A two-sample test for a linear hypothesis whose power is independent of the variance. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 16(3), 243–258. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177731088

See also

ts_fwd_norm_mean; seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal for the known variance sample size.

Other ts_fwd_norm_mean: ts_fwd_norm_mean()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean score on a 100 point skills assessment, to within 2 points.
ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 2, conf_level = 0.95)
#> [1] 10

# A narrow target on a standardized scale: the rule exceeds the minimum.
ts_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 0.1, conf_level = 0.95)
#> [1] 20
